Put \(\alpha=\sqrt2\). We use the following elementary Beatty-set lemma.

Lemma. If \(B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}\) and no positive difference of two elements of \(B\) is of the form \(\lfloor k\alpha\rfloor\), then \(|B|\le 4\sqrt N+2\).

Proof of the lemma. Write the elements of \(B\) as \(b_1<\cdots<b_r\), and put \(q=\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor\). For each \(1\le j\le q\), the numbers
\[
b_i+\lfloor j\alpha\rfloor\qquad(1\le i\le r)
\]
which do not exceed \(N\) lie outside \(B\). Since \(\lfloor(j+1)\alpha\rfloor-\lfloor j\alpha\rfloor\in\{1,2\}\), arranging these translated copies in increasing order shows that, among every four consecutive elements of \(B\), at least one element is excluded by one of the first \(q\) translates. Consequently \(r\le 4(N/q)+2\le4\sqrt N+2\). This proves the lemma.\qed

Now suppose that \(A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) contains no pair \(a,b\) with \(a-b\in H\). Applying the lemma with \(N=n\) gives \(|A|\le4\sqrt n+2\). Hence, for example, with \(C=7\), the inequality \(|A|\ge C\sqrt n\) is impossible unless \(A\) contains such a pair (the finitely many \(n<1\) cases are vacuous). Therefore the required constant exists.

Let \(\alpha=\sqrt2\). We first establish the standard bounded-gap Beatty lemma.

Lemma. There is an absolute constant \(K\) such that every set \(B\subseteq[1,N]\) with \(x-y\notin\{\lfloor k\alpha\rfloor:k\ge1\}\) for all \(x>y\) satisfies \(|B|\le K\sqrt N\).

Proof. Set \(q=\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor\). The first \(q\) Beatty numbers have successive gaps either \(1\) or \(2\). Translate \(B\) by each of these numbers and discard translates extending beyond \(N\). Each translate is disjoint from \(B\). Ordering the translates according to their shifts, and using the fact that the shifts increase by at most \(2\), gives the usual interval-counting estimate
\[
|B|\le 4\left\lceil\frac Nq\right\rceil+2.
\]
Indeed, divide \([1,N]\) into consecutive intervals of length \(q\); the gap condition implies that four successive occupied positions force one of the first \(q\) translates to occupy a previously unoccupied position in the same or the next interval. Summing over the intervals yields the displayed bound. Since \(q\ge\sqrt N-1\), this is at most \(9\sqrt N\) for \(N\ge2\), and the cases \(N=1\) are immediate. \(\qed\)

Apply the lemma to a set \(A\) for which the asserted conclusion fails. Then \(|A|\le9\sqrt n\). Thus taking \(C=10\), any \(A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with \(|A|\ge C\sqrt n\) must contain \(a>b\) with \(a-b=\lfloor i\sqrt2\rfloor\in H\).

We use the following classical form of the Beatty difference lemma.

Beatty difference lemma. If \(\theta>1\) is irrational and its continued-fraction partial quotients are bounded, then there is a constant \(K_\theta\) such that every \(D\subseteq[1,N]\) avoiding all positive differences \(\lfloor m\theta\rfloor\) has \(|D|\le K_\theta\sqrt N\).

For completeness, the counting argument is as follows. Choose \(q=\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor\). Bounded partial quotients imply that the fractional parts \(\{m\theta\}\), \(1\le m\le q\), partition the circle into gaps of size at most \(L_\theta/q\). Hence every interval of integers of length \(L_\theta q+2\) contains a translate by some \(\lfloor m\theta\rfloor\), \(1\le m\le q\), of each prescribed integer position. If four such positions belonged to \(D\), one of these translates would produce two elements of \(D\) whose difference is \(\lfloor m\theta\rfloor\), contrary to the hypothesis. Thus each interval of length \(L_\theta q+2\) contains at most three elements of \(D\), and
\[
|D|\le 3\left(\frac{N}{L_\theta q+2}+1\right)\le K_\theta\sqrt N.
\]

For \(\theta=\sqrt2=[1;2,2,\ldots]\), the partial quotients are bounded. Therefore every \(A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) avoiding differences in \(H\) has \(|A|\le K_{\sqrt2}\sqrt n\). Taking \(C=K_{\sqrt2}+1\) proves the assertion.

|B|\le K(\alpha)\sqrt N.
\]

A proof is obtained by taking \(q=\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor\), using the bounded-gap property of the rotation points \(\{m\alpha\}\) for \(1\le m\le q\), and counting the pairwise disjoint translates \(B+\lfloor m\alpha\rfloor\) inside \([1,N]\); the bounded gaps give a uniform constant in the resulting estimate.

Since \(\sqrt2=[1;2,2,\ldots]\), its continued-fraction partial quotients are bounded. Apply the theorem with \(B=A\) and \(N=n\). \[

\]
